opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I should say up front that reinforcement learning isn't my core area. My background is mostly in computer graphics, physical simulation, and building programming languages and compilers like Taichi. So I see the sparse-reward problem more from the side of someone who builds the environments these agents learn in than from the side of someone designing the algorithms.

From that vantage point, I'd say there's been real progress, but much of it has come from changing the problem rather than solving it head-on. The classic sparse-reward setting is an agent wandering around and getting a signal maybe once in a million steps, and that's still genuinely hard. What people have gotten good at is finding ways around it: reward shaping, curriculum learning, intrinsic motivation and curiosity-style bonuses, hindsight relabeling, learning from demonstrations, and more recently, starting from large pretrained models that already carry a lot of prior knowledge, so exploration isn't starting from zero.

The angle I find most interesting, given my own work, is differentiable simulation. If your physics simulator is differentiable, you can sometimes skip the trial-and-error framing entirely. Instead of waiting for a sparse scalar reward and estimating gradients through lots of noisy rollouts, you backpropagate directly through the dynamics and get a dense, informative gradient about how to change your actions. It doesn't work everywhere. Contact-rich problems, discontinuities, and long horizons can make the gradients badly behaved. But for many control and design problems it turns a needle-in-a-haystack search into a much more tractable optimization.

The other thing I'd emphasize is that simulation speed matters a lot. When rewards are sparse, you need a huge number of samples. If you can run your environment thousands of times faster on a GPU, problems that looked hopeless become feasible just through brute force plus some clever tricks. So part of the progress isn't purely algorithmic. It's infrastructure.

So my overall assessment is cautiously optimistic. We haven't found a universal answer to sparse rewards, and I'm not sure there is one, because at some level it's a fundamental exploration problem. But between better priors, better simulators, and better ways of getting gradient information, the set of problems where it blocks you is shrinking. That's how I'd frame it as an outsider who cares a lot about the tools underneath.

r001.rationale: The response says there is no universal answer and that sparse rewards remain a fundamental exploration problem, so it judges the problem unsolved.

r002.rationale: It mentions starting from large pretrained models to give agents prior knowledge, but does not identify reinforcement-learning fine-tuning as part of that approach.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'll be honest up front: my own work has been more on the simulation and differentiable programming side, with Taichi and the physics engines we built, so I look at sparse rewards partly from the outside, and partly as someone who has spent years trying to get gradients to flow through hard problems.

My assessment is that the field has made real progress, but a lot of it comes from going around the problem rather than solving it head-on.

The direct attacks are things like intrinsic motivation and curiosity, count-based exploration, hindsight experience replay, and curriculum learning. These genuinely work in the settings they were designed for. Hindsight replay in particular was a beautiful idea: if you failed to reach goal A but ended up at state B, just relabel it as a success for goal B. That turns a sparse signal into a dense one almost for free. Curiosity-driven methods let agents make progress in environments like Montezuma's Revenge that were basically hopeless under pure extrinsic reward.

But each of those methods tends to be fragile. Intrinsic rewards can get hijacked by noisy TVs, random pixels that look novel forever. Reward shaping requires a human to encode knowledge, which brings back the very thing RL promised to remove. So I'd say we have a toolbox, not a theory.

The bigger shifts, in my view, came from three indirect directions.

First, large-scale pretraining. If a policy or world model already knows a lot about how the world works, from video, from language, from offline trajectories, then the reward is no longer the only teacher. The sparse signal just needs to steer a prior that is already mostly right. That's a very different regime from tabula rasa RL, and I think much of the apparent progress on sparse rewards is really progress on priors.

Second, differentiable simulation, which is close to my heart. If your environment is differentiable, you don't need the reward to be dense in time, because you can backpropagate through the dynamics and get a gradient from a single terminal outcome. That doesn't scale to everything, contact and discontinuities are painful, but for physical control, it sidesteps exploration entirely in many cases. The sample efficiency gap can be orders of magnitude.

Third, and most recently, learned reward models and verifiers in the language model world. Training reasoning models with a binary signal, correct or incorrect at the end of a long chain, is a sparse-reward problem in disguise, and the fact that it works at all tells you something. It works because the base model already produces reasonable trajectories often enough that the sparse signal has something to grab onto. That is again the prior doing the heavy lifting.

So where does that leave us? I'd say exploration as a pure problem, finding a needle in a haystack with no structure, is still mostly unsolved and may be unsolvable in general. What has changed is that we've become very good at making sure there is structure, either by bringing it in from data, from simulators, or from human-designed curricula. The honest summary is that we didn't make sparse rewards dense. We made agents that need less density.

r001.rationale: The response says that exploration as a pure sparse-reward problem is still mostly unsolved, while describing progress as relying on added structure.

r002.rationale: It describes pretraining as providing a prior that sparse rewards can steer, but does not identify a sequence of pretraining followed by reinforcement-learning fine-tuning as the current approach.

astra-6.text:
I think we’ve made progress, but I wouldn’t say the sparse-reward problem is solved. The difficulty is that an agent can try many things without ever receiving a signal that tells it whether it’s moving in the right direction. If success is the only reward, it may never discover success in the first place.

There are several ways to help: encourage exploration, learn from demonstrations, or start with easier tasks and gradually increase the difficulty. But then the question is how much structure we’re supplying ourselves. Are we getting better at learning from sparse rewards, or are we making the rewards less sparse through our task design?

For me, a strong sign of progress would be an agent that can reliably learn across different long-horizon tasks with very little task-specific guidance. Existing methods offer useful pieces of that, but robust exploration and figuring out which earlier actions deserve credit remain difficult.

r001.rationale: The candidate explicitly says the sparse-reward problem is not solved.

r002.rationale: It mentions exploration, demonstrations, and easier tasks, but does not identify pre-training followed by reinforcement-learning fine-tuning as the current approach.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there has been progress, but sparse rewards are still a major challenge. If an agent only gets feedback when it completes a task, it can spend a huge amount of time exploring without discovering anything useful. And without a successful example, it’s hard to know which actions deserve credit.

There are several ways to make that easier: encourage exploration, start with simpler tasks, or use demonstrations to give the agent a useful starting point. But solving a particular benchmark with those techniques doesn’t necessarily mean we have a general solution.

For me, an important measure of progress is how much guidance we have to provide. Can the agent discover useful behavior with less reward engineering and fewer interactions? That’s a stronger sign of progress than success on a task where we’ve carefully designed all the intermediate rewards.

r001.rationale: It says sparse rewards remain a major challenge and that benchmark success does not establish a general solution, communicating that the problem remains unsolved.

r002.rationale: It mentions exploration, simpler tasks, and demonstrations, but does not identify pre-training followed by reinforcement-learning fine-tuning as the current approach.
